prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- The U.S. military is distributing pamphlets in eastern Afghanistan in an effort to find a soldier who has been missing for more than two weeks, the military said Thursday. A soldier mans a weapon at the rear of a U.S. Army helicopter over Afghanistan in May. The Taliban has claimed responsibility for kidnapping the soldier, who has not been identified, along with three Afghan soldiers. All went missing on June 30 in southeastern Afghanistan. The military believes the soldier may have been moved to various locations, including across the border into Pakistan, U.S. military officials said. There are two versions of the pamphlets, which are in the Pashto language and were made available to CNN by U.S. Forces Afghanistan. One shows the image of an American soldier shaking hands in a group of kids with the message, "One of our American guests is missing. Return the guest to his home. Call us at ..." and lists a phone number. The other shows a U.S. soldier kicking down a door, and then an outstretched hand with the superimposed image of a soldier, his head and arms drooping, and the words, "If you do not release the U.S. soldier then ... you will be hunted," Capt. Elizabeth Mathias, a U.S. military spokeswoman, said Thursday. Soldiers have posted and handed out the pamphlets across Ghazni and Paktia provinces over the past 24 hours, Mathias said. Days after the soldier went missing, a senior U.S. military official said, he and the three missing Afghan soldiers were captured by low-level militants and then quickly "sold" to the clan and network led by warlord Siraj Haqqani, who is believed to be deeply involved in the action. The Haqqani clan operates on both sides of the Afghan-Pakistani border and is well known to the U.S. military. The soldier apparently left his small outpost on his own on June 30 with no apparent means of defending himself, the official said. Taliban commander Mulvi Sangeen said the U.S. soldier visited a military post in the Yousaf Khel district in Paktika province, got drunk, and was ambushed while returning to his car. Sangeen said the soldier was taken to a safe place. Paktika and Paktia provinces are adjacent. CNN could not independently verify Sangeen's claims. A source with the U.S. military denied the claim that the soldier was drunk. "The Taliban are known for lying, and what they are claiming [is] not true," the source said.

*KABUL, Afghanistan* — The U.S. military has distributed pamphlets written in Pashto across parts of eastern Afghanistan as part of an effort to locate an American soldier believed to have been kidnapped by Taliban militants, military officials said.

The soldier, whose name has not been released pending notification and security concerns, went missing from his unit in eastern Afghanistan, an area where Taliban and affiliated insurgent groups have maintained a strong presence.

The leaflets urge local residents to provide information about the soldier’s whereabouts and include instructions on how to contact coalition forces. U.S. officials said the pamphlets were intended to reach villagers in remote areas where insurgents may be moving the soldier or seeking support from local networks.

Taliban spokesmen have claimed responsibility for holding the American, though U.S. military officials have not publicly confirmed the circumstances of his disappearance or the identity of those believed to be holding him.

Search operations are ongoing, according to coalition officials. Troops have been conducting ground searches, intelligence-gathering efforts and outreach to local leaders in the region.

The incident comes amid continued fighting in eastern Afghanistan, where U.S. and Afghan forces have faced persistent attacks from Taliban fighters and other militant groups operating near the border with Pakistan.

Military officials said recovering the missing soldier remains a top priority.

A U.S. soldier has been missing in eastern Afghanistan since June 30, and Taliban militants are claiming they are holding him, according to U.S. military officials and reports from the region.

The soldier disappeared from his base in Paktika province, an area along the volatile Afghanistan-Pakistan border where Taliban insurgents and allied militant groups operate. U.S. officials have not released full details of the circumstances surrounding his disappearance, citing operational security and efforts to recover him safely.

Taliban spokesmen have claimed responsibility for capturing the soldier, saying he is alive and in their custody. The claims have not been independently verified, and U.S. military officials have said they are investigating all reports.

In recent days, pamphlets reportedly posted in parts of **Ghazni** and **Paktia** provinces warned local residents against assisting U.S. or Afghan forces in the search. The leaflets allegedly threatened anyone who provided information about the missing soldier or cooperated with coalition troops.

There are also indications that the **Haqqani network**, a powerful militant faction with close ties to the Taliban and a strong presence in eastern Afghanistan and Pakistan’s tribal areas, may be involved or could have custody of the soldier. U.S. and Afghan officials have long accused the Haqqani network of kidnappings, cross-border attacks, and sheltering foreign fighters.

Coalition forces are continuing search operations, while officials say recovering the missing soldier remains a top priority. The incident comes amid escalating violence in Afghanistan and highlights the risks faced by U.S. troops operating in remote insurgent-controlled areas.

(CNN) -- U.S. forces in eastern Afghanistan are distributing leaflets and using other outreach efforts to seek information about an American soldier who went missing last week, military officials said, as a Taliban commander claimed the insurgent group is holding the service member.

The leaflets, dropped and handed out in areas near where the soldier disappeared, ask Afghans to come forward with tips that could help locate him, according to U.S. military officials. The campaign is part of a broader search effort involving ground forces, intelligence assets and coordination with Afghan authorities.

“The use of leaflets is just one of the many methods we are using to locate our missing soldier,” said Capt. Elizabeth Mathias, a U.S. military spokeswoman. “We are doing everything we can to find him and return him safely.”

The soldier, whose name has not been released by the military pending family notifications and operational considerations, went missing from his unit in eastern Afghanistan. U.S. officials have declined to provide detailed circumstances surrounding his disappearance, citing the ongoing search.

A Taliban commander, Mulvi Sangeen, told reporters that his fighters had captured the soldier and that he was alive. “We have captured an American soldier,” Sangeen said, claiming the service member was being held by Taliban militants in the region.

CNN could not independently verify the Taliban claim or the soldier’s condition.

The disappearance comes amid intensified fighting in Afghanistan, particularly in the east and south, where U.S. and NATO troops have faced persistent attacks from Taliban insurgents and allied militant networks. Eastern Afghanistan’s rugged terrain and porous border with Pakistan have long made search operations difficult.

Military officials said the leaflets are intended to reach villagers, tribal elders and anyone else who may have seen suspicious activity or have knowledge of the soldier’s whereabouts. Such leaflets often include instructions on how to contact coalition forces and may promise confidentiality or rewards for useful information.

Mathias said U.S. forces are urging anyone with knowledge of the missing soldier to come forward. “Any information, no matter how small it may seem, could be important,” she said.

Taliban fighters have previously used captured foreign troops, aid workers and Afghan officials as bargaining chips, sometimes seeking prisoner exchanges, ransom payments or propaganda value. U.S. military officials have not said whether any demands have been made.

The search is continuing, officials said, and commanders in the region are treating the case as a top priority.

**U.S. Soldier, Three Afghan Troops Missing in Southeastern Afghanistan**

*KABUL, Afghanistan* — An American soldier and three Afghan soldiers have gone missing in southeastern Afghanistan, prompting a broad military search and competing claims from U.S. officials and the Taliban about their fate.

The U.S. military said the American service member, whose name was being withheld pending notification of family, disappeared while operating with Afghan forces in a volatile area near the Pakistan border. Three Afghan soldiers assigned to the same mission were also reported missing.

Coalition and Afghan forces launched search operations by ground and air after the troops failed to return or make contact, military officials said. Checkpoints were set up, villages were questioned, and aircraft were used to scan rugged terrain where insurgents have long maintained routes and safe havens.

U.S. officials said they were investigating the circumstances of the disappearance and had not confirmed Taliban claims that the missing personnel had been captured. A military spokesman said the search remained active and that officials were pursuing “all available leads.”

The Taliban, however, issued a conflicting account, claiming its fighters had seized the American soldier and the Afghan troops during an encounter in the region. The insurgent group offered few verifiable details, and its statements could not be independently confirmed.

The disappearance underscores the risks faced by U.S. and Afghan forces operating in southeastern Afghanistan, where mountainous terrain, porous borders and entrenched militant networks have complicated military operations for years.

U.S. commanders said efforts to locate the missing troops would continue and declined to provide further operational details, citing the sensitivity of the search.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

U.S. officials have expressed concern that the soldier could be taken into Pakistan’s tribal areas, where militant networks have historically found refuge and where recovering him would become significantly more difficult.

The military has also pushed back against reports suggesting the soldier may have been drunk when he disappeared. A U.S. military spokesman denied that claim, saying there was no evidence to support it.

The soldier’s disappearance has prompted an intense search effort involving U.S. and Afghan forces, with troops questioning residents, monitoring border routes and distributing the leaflets in an attempt to pressure the captors and gather intelligence.
